items.title: Finite simplicial constructible sheaves have an actual derived incidence model
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $K$ be a finite simplicial complex, $D$ a subcomplex and $X=|K|\setminus|D|$. Let $P$ be the face poset of the open simplices of $K$ not in $D$, ordered by inclusion of faces. The exact realization of finite-dimensional covariant $k$-diagrams on $P$ induces a fully faithful functor into $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$, with essential image the complexes having bounded finite-rank locally constant cohomology on each open simplex. Ordinary and compact-support cohomology, ordinary Hom and internal derived Hom have bounded finite cochain models and commute with every coefficient field extension. For a local product projection $\operatorname{pr}:V\times F\to V$ with supplied finite deleted-boundary models and $B$ in the stated constructible subcategory on the base, there is a natural local comparison $R\operatorname{pr}_*\operatorname{pr}^*B\simeq B\otimes_k C^*(F;k)$, taking the unit to $B\otimes(k\to C^*(F;k))$. This does not assert that an arbitrary algebraic map is simplicial.
items.strategy:
1.1 **The carrier map.** The principal upsets $P_{\ge\sigma}=\{\tau\in P:\tau\supseteq\sigma\}$ form a basis of the Alexandrov topology: a subset is open exactly when it is upward closed, and an upward-closed set is the union of the principal upsets of its elements. Since $D$ is a subcomplex, every face of a simplex in $D$ lies in $D$, so contraposition makes the set $P$ of nonempty simplices outside $D$ upward closed under taking cofaces; hence $q^{-1}(P_{\ge\sigma})=\{x\in X:\sigma\subseteq q(x)\}=\operatorname{St}(\sigma)$, because a point of $|K|$ whose carrier contains $\sigma$ cannot lie in $|D|$ and every coface of a simplex of $P$ again lies in $P$. The star $\operatorname{St}(\sigma)=\bigcup_{\tau\supseteq\sigma}\tau^\circ$ is open in $|K|$, since its trace on each closed simplex $|\eta|$ is $\{x\in|\eta|:\sigma\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(x)\}$, which is relatively open when $\sigma\subseteq\eta$ and empty otherwise; being contained in $X$ it is also open in $X$. As the principal upsets form a basis, $q$ is continuous. Each $\sigma^\circ$ is convex in the affine simplex spanned by $\sigma$, hence connected, locally path-connected and simply connected, and each $\operatorname{St}(\sigma)$ is open and nonempty. [given, F1]

1.2 **Exact realization.** A diagram $V:P\to k\text{-}\mathbf{Vect}$ defines a sheaf $U\mapsto\lim_{\sigma\in U}V_\sigma$: compatible families glue uniquely componentwise. The least neighbourhood $P_{\ge\sigma}$ has initial object $\sigma$, so its sections and its stalk are $V_\sigma$. Conversely, a sheaf on $P$ has these values on the principal opens; restrictions give the diagram, and the sheaf axiom recovers its sections on every open. Thus sheaves on $P$ and diagrams are equivalent. Define $\widehat V=q^{-1}V$. Its stalk at $x$ is $V_{q(x)}$, so realization is exact. On $\sigma^\circ$, the carrier factors through the point $\sigma$ of $P$; composition of inverse images identifies its restriction with the constant sheaf of value $V_\sigma$. This constructs the constant-sheaf identification, rather than inferring it from an abstract equality of stalk values. [given, F2, F3]

1.3 **Triviality and generization.** First, a finite-rank local system on a convex simplex interior is constant. By [F18], subdivide a path into finitely many intervals lying in trivializing opens and compose their stalk identifications. Refining the subdivision does not change the composite. On overlaps, transition matrices are locally constant, so a further subdivision proves independence of the trivializing opens. A homotopy between paths has compact square domain; subdivide that square finely enough that each small square maps into one trivializing open. Transport around each small square is the identity, and cancellation of its shared edges shows that transport along the two boundary paths agrees. Convexity provides such a homotopy between any two paths with fixed endpoints. Transport from a fixed point therefore defines a sheaf map from its constant stalk sheaf to the local system: near each point it is the identification from one trivialization. It is an isomorphism by the stalk criterion. Put $V_\sigma=F_{b_\sigma}$. For $\sigma\le\tau$, represent a germ at $b_\sigma$ on a sufficiently small ambient Euclidean ball; its intersection with $\tau^\circ$ is nonempty and convex. Extend its restriction uniquely along the constant sheaf on $\tau^\circ$ and evaluate at $b_\tau$. Equal germ representatives agree on a smaller such ball, so this map is well defined and linear. The same construction based at any point of $\sigma^\circ$ is locally constant after the canonical transport identifications: lift finitely many basis germs to ambient sections and shrink so that their values on each of the finitely many cofaces are fixed. Connectedness of $\sigma^\circ$ makes each incidence matrix constant throughout it. For $\sigma\le\eta\le\tau$, choose a point of $\eta^\circ$ in the ball representing the original germ and restrict the same section near that point into $\tau^\circ$; uniqueness of extension and the just-proved independence of the point on $\eta^\circ$ give the transitivity equation. Identities are immediate. This reconstructs a diagram functorially from $F$. [given, F1, F2, F6, F18, construct]

1.4 **The standard injectives.** For $\tau\in P$ and a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space $W$ let $I_\tau(W)$ be the diagram with value $W$ at every $\sigma\subseteq\tau$ and $0$ elsewhere, the structure maps being identities where both values are $W$. A diagram map $V\to I_\tau(W)$ is exactly a $k$-linear map $V_\tau\to W$, since its $\tau$-component determines all components and conversely any such linear map extends by the zero maps; therefore $I_\tau(W)$ is injective because $\operatorname{Hom}(-,W)$ is exact. Every diagram $V$ embeds into the finite direct sum $\bigoplus_{\tau\in P}I_\tau(V_\tau)$ by the identity component at $\tau$, a nonzero vector of $V_\tau$ being detected by that component. Hence the finite diagram category has enough injectives and explicit finite injective embeddings, and by [F10] every bounded complex of finite-dimensional diagrams has a bounded injective model whose terms are finite sums of these standard injectives with the stated finite-dimensional ranges. [given, F10]

1.5 **Representables.** The diagram $P_\sigma$ has value $k$ on cofaces of $\sigma$ and zero elsewhere, and $\operatorname{Hom}(P_\sigma,V)=V_\sigma$; hence it is projective and these diagrams generate. On $\operatorname{St}(\sigma)$ its realization is canonically constant, since all its diagram maps there are identities. The extension-by-zero adjunction gives $j_{\sigma!}k_{\operatorname{St}(\sigma)}\to q^{-1}P_\sigma$, identity on that star; both sides have zero stalks elsewhere, so this actual morphism is an isomorphism. The finite projective bar construction of [F10] resolves every bounded finite-dimensional diagram complex by a bounded complex of finite sums of these representables. [given, F2, F3, F5, F10]

1.6 **Internal derived Hom.** For bounded representatives $A,B$, choose a bounded-below injective replacement $B\to J$. By [F16], $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,J)$ represents $R\mathcal Hom(A,B)$ and its derived sections on $U$ represent $R\operatorname{Hom}(A|_U,B|_U)$. The reason ordinary sections suffice in this model is that $\mathcal Hom(A^i,J^j)$ is injective: tensor with a $k$-sheaf is exact stalkwise and its right adjoint is sheaf Hom. There are finitely many $A$-degrees in each Hom degree. Restriction preserves injectives by its exact left adjoint $j_!$. Taking the exact filtered colimit of the section complexes therefore gives $\mathcal H^r(R\mathcal Hom(A,B))_x=\varinjlim_{U\ni x}\operatorname{Hom}_{D(U)}(A|_U,B|_U[r])$. Boundedness will follow from the local finite models. [given, F5, F11, F16]

2.1 **Sections on a star.** The generization maps of step 1.3 are locally constant along each face: trivialize the finite-rank restriction near a point of that face, lift its finitely many basis germs to ambient sections, and shrink one neighbourhood where their restrictions to each of the finitely many incident cofaces are constant. Their coface matrices are then constant on that face neighbourhood. Since each face interior is connected, these local matrices define the same transported map throughout it; restrictions through nested faces compose as in step 1.3. For $\sigma\in P$, a section on $\operatorname{St}(\sigma)$ with zero germ at $b_\sigma$ vanishes on a nonempty subset of every incident open simplex, hence on that whole simplex by [F6], so it is zero. Conversely, start with a germ $a\in F_{b_\sigma}$ and define its value along every $\tau^\circ$ with $\tau\supseteq\sigma$ by the generization map followed by the unique constant transport on $\tau^\circ$. At a point of $\eta^\circ$, lift that assigned germ to an ambient local section. Its values on every incident $\tau^\circ$ are the prescribed ones, by the local constant matrices and their composition rule; shrinking finitely many times ensures agreement for all cofaces. Thus the assigned family of germs is locally represented by ambient sections. These sections agree stalkwise on their overlaps and glue by the sheaf axiom to a section on the whole star. This proves $F(\operatorname{St}(\sigma))\cong F_{b_\sigma}$. The simplex interiors were not treated as open subsets of the star. [given, F2, F6, step 1.3]

2.2 **Compact-support reduction.** Extend $V$ by zero to the full face poset $P_K$, obtaining $\widetilde V$; no arrow goes from a retained face to a deleted coface because $D$ is a subcomplex. The restriction of $q_K^{-1}\widetilde V$ to $X$ is canonically $q^{-1}V$. The open extension-by-zero adjunction gives $j_!q^{-1}V\to q_K^{-1}\widetilde V$; it is the identity on $X$, and both sides have zero stalks on $|D|$, so it is an isomorphism. The space $X$ is locally compact Hausdorff: its finite Euclidean realization is compact Hausdorff and $X$ is open. Thus [F15] and compactness give $R\Gamma_c(X,q^{-1}V)\simeq R\Gamma(|K|,q_K^{-1}\widetilde V)$. [given, F1, F2, F5, F15, step 1.2]

2.3 **The product pair.** Let $V=|K_V|\setminus|D_V|$ and $F=|K_F|\setminus|D_F|$ be realizations of finite pairs with face posets $P_V,P_F$ as in the statement, let $\operatorname{pr}:V\times F\to V$ be the projection, and let $B$ be a bounded complex of finite-dimensional diagrams on $P_V$, realized as $A:=q_V^{-1}B$, with the product realized along $q_{V\times F}:V\times F\to P_V\times P_F$. The product $|K_V|\times|K_F|$ has the finite regular product-cell decomposition whose closed cells are the convex polytopes $|\sigma|\times|\eta|$; the star, diagram and acyclicity arguments apply verbatim to these regular cells, using their convex faces, so no product of simplices is asserted to be a simplex, and $V\times F$ is the complement of the subcomplex $D$ consisting of the cells lying in $|D_V|\times|K_F|$ or in $|K_V|\times|D_F|$; a product cell $\sigma\times\eta$ lies outside $D$ exactly when $\sigma\notin D_V$ and $\eta\notin D_F$, so its poset is exactly $P_V\times P_F$, and $\operatorname{pr}^*A=q_{V\times F}^{-1}(B\boxtimes k)$, where $B\boxtimes k$ denotes the product diagram with value $B_\sigma$ at $(\sigma,\eta)$ and the identity in the $\eta$-variable. [given, F1, F2, step 1.2]

2.4 **Realized injectives are acyclic on stars.** Put $Z_\tau=|\tau|\cap X$, closed in $X$. The restriction of $q^{-1}I_\tau(W)$ to $Z_\tau$ is canonically constant: the restricted diagram has value $W$ and identity maps everywhere. Its stalks vanish off $Z_\tau$, so the actual closed-inclusion unit of [F8] identifies it with $i_{\tau*}W_{Z_\tau}$. Consequently its cohomology on an open $U$ is the constant-sheaf cohomology of $U\cap Z_\tau$. For $U=\operatorname{St}(\sigma)$ this intersection is empty unless $\sigma\le\tau$; otherwise it is the convex set in $|\tau|$ where all coordinates indexed by $\sigma$ are positive, and cannot meet $D$. It has cohomology $W$ in degree zero and zero above by [F7]. Globally $Z_\tau$ contracts to $b_\tau$: at positive time the segment from a retained point to $b_\tau$ lies in $\tau^\circ$. It has a contractible-open neighbourhood basis, being open in the convex simplex $|\tau|$. Hence its constant-sheaf cohomology is also $W$ in degree zero and zero above. This proves ordinary global and star acyclicity of realized standard injectives and their finite sums. It does not claim that they are injective or c-soft among all sheaves. [given, F2, F3, F7, F8, step 1.4]

3.1 **The ordinary equivalence.** The constructions of steps 1.2 and 1.3 are inverse equivalences between finite-dimensional covariant $k$-diagrams on $P$ and sheaves on $X$ whose restriction to every open simplex is locally constant of finite rank. On the diagram side, the reconstruction of $\widehat V$ has $V_\sigma(\widehat V)=(\widehat V)_{b_\sigma}\cong V_\sigma$ by step 1.2, and the generization maps of step 1.3 reproduce the maps of $V$, since the canonical sections over the stars have the prescribed values. On the sheaf side, the canonical morphism $\widehat{V(F)}\to F$ is adjunct to the family $V_\sigma\cong F(\operatorname{St}(\sigma))$ of inverse isomorphisms from step 2.1 and is an isomorphism on stalks by steps 1.2, 1.3 and 2.1, hence an isomorphism by [F2]. Both functors are exact: realization is exact by step 1.2, and reconstruction is exact because a sequence of such sheaves is exact exactly when it is exact at the stalks, which by step 1.3 are the values of the reconstructed diagrams and the generization maps are functorial, so a diagram sequence is exact exactly when the corresponding sheaf sequence is. [given, F2, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1]

3.2 **Ordinary cohomology models.** Dualizing the finite projective bar resolution of [F10] on the opposite poset gives a bounded injective model $V\to I$ with terms finite sums of standard injectives. Realization is exact, and step 2.4 makes these terms acyclic for global sections and for every retained star. The acyclic-resolution comparison [F13] consequently gives $R\Gamma(\operatorname{St}(\sigma),q^{-1}V)\simeq I_\sigma\simeq V_\sigma$ and $R\Gamma(X,q^{-1}V)\simeq\lim_{\sigma\in P}I_\sigma$. Here its bounded-complex version follows by resolving the finitely many source degrees and filtering the total complex; the sheaf-level comparisons of [F13] identify each graded piece, hence the total. All syzygies lie in the whole field-sheaf category covered by [F11], and AC supplies DC. This last complex is a bounded finite-dimensional cochain model. Equivalently the bar model of [F10] has incidence terms $\prod_{\sigma_0<\cdots<\sigma_p}V_{\sigma_p}$ and its coefficient and face differential. Its finite matrix construction commutes with every field extension. If $P$ is empty then $X$ is empty, both categories and all these models are zero; no nonempty-poset supplier is applied in that case. [given, F3, F9, F10, F11, F13, step 2.4]

4.1 **An acyclic product resolution.** In the setting of step 2.3, choose bounded diagram-injective models $B\to I$ and $k\to J$ on $P_V$ and $P_F$. The signed total $I\boxtimes J$ realizes a resolution of $\operatorname{pr}^*A$: over a field tensor is exact, and the finite double-complex filtration proves the augmentation is a quasi-isomorphism. Each elementary term is the closed pushforward of the constant coefficient $W\otimes U$ on $Z_\tau\times Z_\nu$. At a point of $V$, take small ambient Euclidean balls meeting only cofaces of its carrier. Their intersections with $Z_\tau$ are empty or convex; $Z_\nu$ is contractible by step 2.4. The constant-polyhedral comparison gives no higher cohomology on the corresponding support intersection in the inverse image of the ball. Taking stalk colimits in an injective direct-image model shows that these terms are $\operatorname{pr}_*$-acyclic. Their ordinary direct images are $i_{\tau*}(W\otimes U)_{Z_\tau}$: on any open base set a locally constant function on its product with the nonempty connected $Z_\nu$ is constant in the fibre, and evaluation at one fibre point identifies it with a locally constant function on the base support. Thus termwise pushforward of this resolution is canonically $q_V^{-1}I\otimes_k C^\bullet(F;k)$, where $C^\bullet(F;k)=\lim_{\nu\in P_F}J_\nu$ is the finite model for $R\Gamma(F,k)$ from step 3.2. This keeps every internal degree of the bounded complex $B$; no degree-zero assumption on $B$ is made. For empty $F$, both the pushforward and $C^\bullet(F;k)$ are zero. [given, F7, F10, F13, F16, F17, step 2.3, step 2.4, step 3.2]

4.2 **The derived carrier unit.** By step 2.1, the actual unit $V\to q_*q^{-1}V$ is an isomorphism on every principal open: its map to the germ at $b_\sigma$ is the identity of $V_\sigma$. Evaluation on a principal open is exact in the sheaf category on $P$, by its diagram description in step 1.2. Consequently, for an injective replacement $q^{-1}V\to J$, the $\sigma$-component of $R^jq_*q^{-1}V$ is $H^j(\operatorname{St}(\sigma),q^{-1}V)$, zero for $j>0$ by step 3.2. Thus the derived unit is an isomorphism for a diagram sheaf. Finite truncation triangles extend the same conclusion to every bounded diagram complex. This argument concerns principal opens in $P$; it makes no assertion that open stars form a neighbourhood basis in $X$. [given, F2, F4, F14, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.2]

4.3 **The compact-support cochain model.** Apply the argument of steps 2.4 and 3.2 to the pair $(K,\varnothing)$, whose face poset is $P_K$ and whose realization is the compact space $|K|$: for a bounded complex $\widetilde V$ of finite-dimensional diagrams on $P_K$, choose a bounded injective resolution $\widetilde V\to J^\bullet$ with terms finite sums of standard injectives [F10], realize it, use the acyclicity of realized standard injectives for $\Gamma(|K|,-)$ from step 2.4, and apply the acyclic-resolution theorem [F13]; the outcome is that $R\Gamma\bigl(|K|,q_K^{-1}\widetilde V\bigr)$ is computed by the finite-dimensional bounded complex $\varprojlim_{\eta\in P_K}J^\bullet_\eta$, with the range bound of [F10] for the poset $P_K$ and its coefficient range. By step 2.2 this complex is a bounded finite cochain model for the compact-support cohomology $R\Gamma_c(X,q^{-1}V)$, and as in step 3.2 every map in the construction is $k$-linear between finite-dimensional spaces, so the model and hence the cohomology commute with every coefficient field extension by [F10]. [given, F10, F13, step 2.4, step 2.2, step 3.2]

5.1 **Product comparison and unit.** The acyclic resolution of step 4.1 identifies $R\operatorname{pr}_*\operatorname{pr}^*A$ with $q_V^{-1}I\otimes_kC^\bullet(F;k)$. The augmentation $B\to I$ and exact tensor over $k$ identify the latter with $A\otimes_kC^\bullet(F;k)$, giving the claimed natural isomorphism. Naturality and restriction compatibility follow from the diagram maps, the termwise direct-image identification and the canonical acyclic-resolution comparisons; they do not rely on testing all-sheaf stalks on whole stars. The adjunction unit is represented by $B\to I$ tensored with the fibre augmentation $k\to C^\bullet(F;k)$. It is therefore $A\otimes(k\to C^\bullet(F;k))$ under the comparison. After full faithfulness and the essential-image argument below, this applies to every $A$ in the stated constructible subcategory; in the Statement this realized base object is denoted $B$. [F10, F13, F16, step 4.1]

5.2 **Derived full faithfulness.** For bounded diagram complexes $U,W$, take a finite projective bar model $P\to U$ and an injective replacement $q^{-1}W\to J$. By [F11], [F12] and the inverse/direct-image adjunction, the Hom complex from $q^{-1}P$ to $J$ equals the Hom complex from $P$ to $q_*J$. The derived carrier unit of step 4.2 identifies $q_*J$ with $W$. Since the bounded projective model $P$ is K-projective, taking degree-zero cohomology identifies $\operatorname{Hom}_{D(X)}(q^{-1}U,q^{-1}W)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_{D(P)}(U,W)$, naturally and compatibly with realization. Shifts give the same comparison in every degree, and [F14] identifies the bounded localizations with their full subcategories. Thus realization is fully faithful. [given, F3, F10, F11, F12, F14, step 1.5, step 4.2]

6.1 **The qualified cone estimate.** Suppose in addition that the fibre augmentation $k\to H^0(F;k)$ is an isomorphism (for these finite models, $F$ nonempty and connected), and that $H^r(F;k)=0$ for $1\le r\le R$. Then $\widetilde C=\operatorname{Cone}(k\to C^\bullet(F;k))$ has no cohomology in degrees $\le R$, including degree $-1$. For $A\in D^{\ge b}$, the Künneth formula gives $H^n(A\otimes\widetilde C)=\bigoplus_{p+r=n}H^p(A)\otimes H^r(\widetilde C)$ stalkwise; a nonzero term requires $p\ge b$ and $r\ge R+1$. The cone of the unit therefore lies in $D^{\ge b+R+1}$. Without the degree-zero condition the estimate is false, for example for a two-point fibre and $A=k$: the unit has cokernel $k$ in degree zero. The product comparison itself needs no connectedness condition and remains local to the supplied models. [given, F17, step 5.1]

6.2 **Finite Hom and scalar extension.** Full faithfulness identifies actual derived Hom with the finite diagram Hom model of [F10]. Its terms are finite products of $\operatorname{Hom}_k(V_\sigma,W_\tau)$ from finite-dimensional coefficient spaces. Tensor with a field extension commutes with these Hom spaces, finite sums, and the matrices and cohomology of the bounded model. This proves the Hom and scalar-extension clauses. The analytic injective replacement $J$ in step 5.2 need not have finite-dimensional terms; it is the equivalent diagram model that is finite. [given, F10, step 5.2]

6.3 **The essential image.** First, if $V$ is a bounded complex of diagrams, then each cohomology sheaf of $q^{-1}V$ is $q^{-1}(H^jV)$ by exactness of $q^{-1}$, and its restriction to an open simplex in $P$ is constant of finite rank, so such complexes lie in the stated image and have bounded finite-rank locally constant cohomology on each open simplex. Conversely, let $A$ be a bounded complex on $X$ whose cohomology sheaves are finite-rank locally constant on every open simplex. By step 3.1 each $H^j(A)$ is isomorphic to $q^{-1}V_j$ for a finite-dimensional diagram $V_j$, and $V_j=0$ outside a finite range of degrees. We build $A$ inductively from its cohomology. If $A$ has at most one nonzero cohomology sheaf, then $A\cong H^n(A)[-n]\cong q^{-1}\bigl(V_n[-n]\bigr)$, using that $q^{-1}$ commutes with shifts up to canonical isomorphism because it is exact. Otherwise let $m$ be the least degree with $H^m(A)\neq0$; the canonical truncation triangle of [F14] reads $H^m(A)[-m]\to A\to\tau^{\ge m+1}A\to H^m(A)[-m+1]$. By induction on the number of nonzero cohomology degrees, $\tau^{\ge m+1}A\cong q^{-1}W$ for a bounded diagram complex $W$, and $H^m(A)[-m]\cong q^{-1}\bigl(V_m[-m]\bigr)$; by step 5.2 the connecting morphism $\delta:q^{-1}W\to q^{-1}(V_m[-m+1])$ is $q^{-1}(\delta_0)$ for a unique morphism $\delta_0$ of the diagram derived category. Completing $\delta_0$ to a distinguished triangle $V_m[-m]\to Y\to W\to V_m[-m+1]$ of [F14] and applying the exact functor $q^{-1}$ yields a triangle $q^{-1}(V_m[-m])\to q^{-1}Y\to q^{-1}W\to q^{-1}(V_m[-m+1])$ whose connecting morphism is $\delta$; two distinguished triangles with isomorphic first two objects and the same connecting morphism are isomorphic, so $A\cong q^{-1}Y$ and $A$ is realized. Hence the essential image is exactly the full subcategory of complexes with bounded finite-rank locally constant cohomology on each open simplex. [given, F2, F14, step 3.1, step 5.2]

6.4 **Local internal-Hom models.** For $x\in\sigma^\circ$, sufficiently small ambient Euclidean balls $U$ in $X$ lie in $\operatorname{St}(\sigma)$ and meet exactly the cofaces $Q_\sigma=\{\tau:\tau\ge\sigma\}$. For realized diagram complexes $A=q^{-1}V$, $B=q^{-1}W$, their restrictions are realized by the same restricted diagrams on $Q_\sigma$. The derived carrier-unit argument applies on $U$: for $\eta\le\tau$ in $Q_\sigma$, $U\cap\operatorname{St}(\eta)\cap|\tau|$ is empty or convex, so the restricted standard-injective resolution is acyclic on every restricted principal star. Consequently step 5.2 identifies $\operatorname{Hom}_{D(U)}(A|_U,B|_U[r])$ with the finite diagram Hom cohomology on $Q_\sigma$. Restriction to smaller such balls is the identity on these finite models. No convexity of an entire open star is required. By step 1.6 the stalk of internal Hom is therefore this same finite model. These identifications also prove local constancy along $\sigma^\circ$, rather than only equality of stalk dimensions: a class on one such ball maps canonically into the cohomology sheaf, and its restrictions to smaller balls about nearby points of $\sigma^\circ$ are the identical diagram class. This defines a map from the constant finite-model cohomology sheaf on $U\cap\sigma^\circ$ to the restricted internal-Hom cohomology sheaf, isomorphic on every stalk, hence an isomorphism. [given, F2, F7, F10, step 1.6, step 2.4, step 5.2]

7.1 **Boundedness and field extension of internal Hom.** The models $\operatorname{Ext}^q_{\operatorname{Diag}(Q_\sigma)}(V|_{Q_\sigma},W|_{Q_\sigma})$ are finite-dimensional and vanish outside a range depending only on the internal amplitude of $V,W$ and the chain length of $Q_\sigma$, whose strict-chain length is at most that of $P$; since $P$ is finite and $Q_\sigma$ depends only on the simplex $\sigma$, the ranges are uniformly bounded over $\sigma$ and over points of $\sigma^\circ$, so $R\mathcal{H}om(A,B)$ is bounded with finite-rank locally constant cohomology. By [F10] the diagram Hom models commute with every field extension, and the identifications of step 6.4 use only the finite models, so extending scalars carries the internal-Hom models to the models of the extended objects. This proves the internal-Hom clause. [given, F10, step 6.4]

8.1 The ordinary equivalence is step 3.1; ordinary cohomology is step 3.2; compact supports are steps 2.2 and 4.3; full faithfulness, finite Hom and the essential image are steps 5.2, 6.2 and 6.3; internal derived Hom is steps 6.4 and 7.1; and the product comparison and qualified cone estimate are steps 5.1 and 6.1. AC is used through injective and comparison suppliers, whereas the finite bar construction itself is choice-free. Neither arbitrary analytic injectives nor arbitrary sheaf sections are asserted finite-dimensional. [given, F10, F11, F13, F16, F17, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 2.2, step 4.3, step 5.2, step 6.2, step 6.3, step 6.4, step 7.1, step 5.1, step 6.1] ∎

items.title: Locally split Cech nerves give actual derived Cartesian sheaf descent
items.statement: Assume AC. For a strict augmented simplicial space $Z_\bullet\to S$, its category of simplicial analytic $k$-sheaves has explicit coinduced injective resolutions. The derived augmentation is computed by a normalized double complex; before normalization its spectral sequence has first page $R^j q_{p*}F_p$ and alternating face differential. A common internal lower bound makes every total-degree diagonal finite. The same construction works for strict bisimplicial diagrams and is compatible with composition of derived right adjoints to exact inverse image. If $Z_\bullet$ is the Čech nerve of a map $P\to S$ admitting local sections, inverse image gives an equivalence from $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(S))$ to the full derived subcategory with Cartesian cohomology. For algebraic principal $\mathrm{GL}$ bundles of separated finite-type complex varieties (Zariski locally trivial bundles) this restricts to the algebraically constructible subcategories, with constructibility required at every simplicial level.
items.strategy:
1.1 **The category and the augmentation.** A simplicial sheaf consists of the $F_p$ and maps $Z_\alpha^{-1}F_p\to F_m$ specified in the Given, with identity and composition identities. Since inverse image is exact, kernels, cokernels and exactness are levelwise; products and coproducts are levelwise with the induced structure maps, so this is an abelian, locally small category with AB3 and AB3*. Define $q^*B$ levelwise by $q_p^{-1}B$, and define $q_*F$ as the equalizer of the two face maps $q_{0*}F_0\rightrightarrows q_{1*}F_1$. A map into this equalizer gives compatible maps at every level by the vertex projections: the equalizer condition makes all vertex choices agree, and the simplicial identities give compatibility with every operator. The inverse/direct-image adjunction therefore gives $q^*\dashv q_*$; $q^*$ is exact. [given, F1, F2]

1.2 **Coinduction and levelwise injectivity.** Set $(N_pI)_m=\prod_{\alpha:[m]\to[p]}(Z_\alpha)_*I$, with structure maps induced by composition. The identity component gives $\operatorname{Hom}(F,N_pI)=\operatorname{Hom}(F_p,I)$; hence $N_pI$ is injective for injective $I$. Functorial embeddings $F_p\hookrightarrow I_p$ give $F\hookrightarrow\prod_pN_pI_p$, detected by the identity component at each level. AC and [F4] make this product injective. Each level of $N_pI$ is a finite product of direct images of injectives, hence injective by [F2], [F4]; the same holds for each level of $\prod_pN_pI_p$. Any injective simplicial sheaf is a retract of its such embedding and is consequently injective at each level. Iteration on cokernels resolves sheaves; the bounded-below replacement construction of [F3], using these explicit embeddings at its successive stages, resolves complexes without changing a supplied lower bound. [F2, F3, F4, F7]

2.1 **The augmented cochain complex of an injective.** For $N_pI$ put $A=q_{p*}I$. Its degree-$m$ augmentation cochains are $A^{\operatorname{Hom}_\Delta([m],[p])}$, with the alternating face differential. The augmentation $A\to A^{p+1}$ sends $a$ to the constant tuple. On cochains define $(hc)(i_0,\ldots,i_{m-1})=c(0,i_0,\ldots,i_{m-1})$ and in degree zero evaluate at vertex $0$. Deleting the inserted vertex gives the identity and all other deletions cancel in pairs, so $dh+hd=\mathrm{id}$ on the augmented complex. Products of these contractions and their restrictions to retracts give an exact augmented complex $0\to q_*J\to q_{0*}J_0\to q_{1*}J_1\to\cdots$ for every injective simplicial sheaf $J$. This is horizontal exactness, not a claim that the derived functors vanish on an arbitrary pulled-back complex. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 **Ordinary Cartesian descent.** Cartesian means that every structure map is an isomorphism. For a Cartesian sheaf $F$ and a local section $s_i:V_i\to P$, put $B_i=s_i^{-1}F_0$. The two face maps to $F_1$ identify the pullbacks of $F_0$ along the two projections. Pulling this identification back by $z\mapsto(s_i(q(z)),z)$ gives $q^{-1}B_i\simeq F_0$ over $q^{-1}V_i$; vertex projections then give $q_p^{-1}B_i\simeq F_p$. On overlaps, pull the same identification back by $(s_i,s_j):V_i\cap V_j\to P\times_S P$. The degree-two identities give the cocycle equation on triple overlaps, and the diagonal degeneracy gives the identity equation. The sheaf axiom glues the $B_i$ to $B$ on $S$ and their identifications to $q^*B\simeq F$. The same construction glues morphisms, so it is an equivalence of ordinary sheaf categories onto Cartesian sheaves. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 **Normalization.** For a cosimplicial abelian object $C$ set $N^nC=\bigcap_{i=0}^{n-1}\ker s^i$ and $T_rC^n=\bigcap_{i=0}^{\min(r,n)-1}\ker s^i$, so $T_0C=C$. The alternating differential preserves $T_r$: applying $s^i$ to it cancels the $i$th and $(i+1)$st faces, and all remaining terms contain $s^{i-1}$ or $s^i$. In degree $n>r$, the map $s^r$ carries $T_rC^n$ into $T_rC^{n-1}$ and vanishes on $T_{r+1}$. For $c\in T_rC^n$ the cosimplicial identities give $(ds^r+s^rd)c=\sum_{j=0}^{r}(-1)^j d^j s^r c$. Multiplying by $(-1)^r$ gives $c$ modulo $T_{r+1}$: all earlier codegeneracies vanish on the difference, and applying $s^r$ kills the terms $j<r$ and identifies the last term with $s^rc$. Thus $(-1)^rs^r$ contracts the quotient $T_r/T_{r+1}$, with zero maps where $n\le r$ and the quotient is zero. Each inclusion $T_{r+1}\hookrightarrow T_r$ is a quasi-isomorphism. For a fixed cohomological degree $n$, these complexes stabilize in degrees $n-1,n,n+1$ once $r\ge n+1$, giving $NC\hookrightarrow C$ a quasi-isomorphism. Finally, successively applying $1-d^{i+1}s^i$ for $i=0,\ldots,n-1$ gives a natural projection onto $N^nC$: it kills the $i$th codegeneracy and preserves those already killed. A surjection of cosimplicial objects lifts a normalized element by first lifting it and then applying this projection; kernels are immediate. Hence $N^n$ is exact, and the normalized first page is $N^p(R^jq_{\bullet*}F_\bullet)$, rather than the unnormalized term $R^jq_{p*}F_p$. [step 2.1, algebra, construct]

4.1 **The derived total model.** Choose $F\to J$ as in step 1.2, with $J^j=0$ for $j<a$. Put $D^{p,j}=q_{p*}J_p^j$ and total differential $d_h+(-1)^p d_v$, where $d_h$ is the alternating face differential. The differentials commute before this sign, so the total differential squares to zero. Step 2.1 identifies the horizontal cohomology with $q_*J^j$ in horizontal degree zero; filtering the bounded-below double complex therefore identifies its total with $q_*J$, which represents $Rq_*F$. Levelwise injectivity from step 1.2 identifies vertical cohomology with $R^jq_{p*}F_p$. Filtration by the simplicial degree $p$ gives the unnormalized first page $E_1^{p,j}=R^jq_{p*}F_p$ and its alternating face differential. Only $0\le p\le n-a$ occurs in total degree $n$, so [F5] gives convergence without completion. Step 3.1 normalizes the horizontal direction without changing the total object. This model also works with any bounded-below levelwise injective replacement: resolve its terms further in the simplicial category and use the vertical acyclic-resolution comparison; finite diagonal filtrations identify both totals. [F3, F5, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 **Bisimplicial diagrams and composition.** Coinduce in both simplicial directions, using products indexed by pairs of operators. The two contractions of step 2.1 identify the doubly augmented total with the derived augmentation. With indices $p,r\ge0$ and $j\ge a$, only finitely many triples satisfy $p+r+j=n$; hence iterated and simultaneous totals agree, with differential signs $d_p+(-1)^pd_r+(-1)^{p+r}d_j$. For a composition of right adjoints $f_*,g_*$ whose inverse-image left adjoints are exact, both right adjoints preserve injectives. A single injective replacement $J$ therefore computes $R(gf)_*F=g_*f_*J$ and $Rg_*Rf_*F$ alike. The comparison respects units and counits because the underived adjunctions compose; its total models are the finite-diagonal models just constructed. [F2, F3, F5, step 2.1, step 4.1]

5.2 **A local section contracts the derived model.** For the Čech nerve over a section domain $V$, set $Z_{-1}=V$ and $e_{-1}=s$. Inserting $s$ as first coordinate gives $e_p:Z_p|_V\to Z_{p+1}|_V$ with $d_0e_p=\mathrm{id}$ and $d_{i+1}e_p=e_{p-1}d_i$ (including the augmentation). The augmented diagram $q_p^{-1}B$, with value $B|_V$ at level $-1$, has canonical structure maps also for these insertions. Resolve it in the enlarged small diagram category generated by the ordinary operators and the $e_p$, with their actual relations. The construction of step 1.2 applies there: coinduction uses products over arrows, and every evaluation of an injective is injective, since each coinduced evaluation is a product of direct images of injectives. Thus we obtain a bounded-below resolution $J$ which retains all $e_p$ and is injective at every level, including $-1$. The insertion maps induce $h:q_{p+1*}J_{p+1}\to q_{p*}J_p$, with $q_{0*}J_0\to J_{-1}$ induced by $s$. The displayed face identities give $d_hh+hd_h=\mathrm{id}$ on each augmented row, and $h$ commutes with $d_v$. They therefore contract the augmented total, which by step 4.1 computes the derived augmentation. Its level-$-1$ complex resolves $B|_V$, so the actual unit $B|_V\to Rq_*q^*B|_V$ is an isomorphism. Restriction to $V$ preserves injectives in the simplicial category: levelwise extension by zero is an exact left adjoint, with structure maps obtained from pullback of extension by zero along the operators. The local calculations consequently compute the restriction of the global unit. They glue to $B\simeq Rq_*q^*B$; for a sheaf $B$ this implies $R^jq_*q^*B=0$ for $j>0$. [F2, F3, F4, F9, step 1.2, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 **Derived full faithfulness and the image.** Derived adjunction and step 5.2 give $\operatorname{Hom}_D(q^*A,q^*B)=\operatorname{Hom}_D(A,Rq_*q^*B)=\operatorname{Hom}_D(A,B)$. By [F6] this also holds in bounded derived categories. Exactness of $q^*$ shows that its image has Cartesian cohomology. Conversely, step 2.2 descends each cohomology sheaf of a bounded object with Cartesian cohomology. Induct on the finitely many nonzero cohomology degrees, using the canonical truncation triangles of [F6]. At each stage full faithfulness lifts the connecting morphism between the already descended objects; its cone realizes the next truncation. Cone triangles with the same connecting morphism are isomorphic by the triangulated axioms, so this induction realizes the original object. [F2, F6, step 5.2, step 2.2]

7.1 **Algebraic constructibility.** An algebraic principal $\mathrm{GL}$ bundle here is Zariski locally trivial; finite type allows a finite algebraic trivializing cover $V_i$ with algebraic sections $s_i$. Inverse image of a locally constant finite-rank sheaf is locally constant of the same finite rank: pull back a trivialization and use the stalk formula. More generally, inverse image along an algebraic map preserves algebraic constructibility. Indeed, the inverse images of a witnessing stratification form a finite partition by locally closed algebraic sets; apply the finite smooth frontier refinement of [F8] to their closures and boundaries. On each resulting stratum the sheaf is the inverse image of one of the original local systems. This argument applies to $q_p$ and to $s_i$. Thus if $F_0$ is algebraically constructible, the descended $B$ is so on each $V_i$. For a single global witnessing stratification, regard all the local strata as locally closed subsets of $S$, prescribe their closures and boundaries and the complements of the $V_i$, and refine by [F8]; every global stratum lies inside one $V_i$ and one local stratum. There are only finitely many cohomology degrees, so one such refinement handles them all. Conversely, if $B$ is constructible, every $q_p^*B$ is constructible by the same argument. This proves the restriction of step 6.1 to objects constructible at each simplicial level; no common finite stratification across infinitely many levels is assumed. [F2, F8, step 2.2, step 6.1]

8.1 Steps 1.2 and 4.1 give the coinduced resolutions and derived augmentation model, step 5.1 gives the bisimplicial and composition clauses, and steps 5.2, 6.1 and 7.1 give locally split Cartesian descent and its algebraic restriction. AC is used for injective data, products of injectives, DC for complex replacements, and the algebraic refinement supplier. No proper-descent conclusion is inferred from local-section descent. [F3, F4, F7, F8, step 1.2, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 5.2, step 6.1, step 7.1] ∎

items.title: Derived tensor–Hom and inverse/direct image for field sheaves
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map of topological spaces and let $k$ be a field. Inverse image of sheaves of $k$-vector spaces ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]], [[def-inverse-image-presheaf-and-sheaf]]) is exact and $f^*\dashv Rf_*$, where $Rf_*$ is computed on bounded-below $k$-linear injective replacements ([[lem-bounded-below-complexes-admit-injective-replacements]], [[thm-injective-complexes-model-the-bounded-below-derived-category]]). For bounded complexes $A,B$ ([[def-bounded-bounded-below-and-bounded-above-complex]]) the derived tensor over $k$ is their signed total tensor ([[def-sheaf-tensor-product]]), and for bounded $A$ and bounded-below $B$ the derived internal Hom $R\mathcal Hom(A,B)$ is computed by $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,I_B)$ in a $k$-linear bounded-below injective model $B\to I_B$ ([[def-sheaf-hom]], [[def-derived-hom-in-the-bounded-setting]]). Flasque $k$-sheaves ([[def-flasque-sheaf]]) are acyclic for sections on every open set ([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]). The tensor-Hom adjunction and the dg associativity, evaluation and symmetry identities are natural. No bounded-constructibility claim for the internal Hom is made here; that requires the local geometric supplier of the later constructible items.
items.strategy: Assume AC. Route: read the ordinary operations off stalks, construct the signed total tensor and the injective Hom model, prove flasque acyclicity from the flasque-kernel lifting theorem, and finish with the chain-Hom adjunction. Sources: Verdier, expose 300, SS1 pp. 339-341 (injective models in $D^+$ and the basic properties of $f_!$) and Stacks Project, Cohomology of Sheaves, SS12 (Definition 12.1, Lemma 12.2, Lemma 12.3, Lemma 12.5). Step 1 (inverse and direct image). The stalk of $f^{-1}G$ at $x$ is $G_{f(x)}$ ([[lem-stalk-inverse-image-sheaf]]), so $f^*=f^{-1}$ is exact and preserves quasi-isomorphisms; the inverse/direct-image adjunction ([[thm-inverse-direct-image-adjunction]]) is $k$-linear, and for injective $I$ on $X$ the functor $\operatorname{Hom}_Y(-,f_*I)$ is naturally $\operatorname{Hom}_X(f^*(-),I)$, so $f_*I$ is injective and the chain-Hom adjunction gives $f^*\dashv Rf_*$ on $D^+$. Step 2 (tensor). Define $F\otimes_kG$ by sheafifying the sectionwise tensor presheaf; its stalks are $F_x\otimes_kG_x$ ([[def-sheaf-tensor-product]]) because filtered colimits commute with finite tensor expressions. All $k$-vector spaces are flat, so tensoring is stalk-exact, and a bounded complex is K-flat: filter the finite-column total tensor against an acyclic complex by $A$-degree and use that each column is acyclic. Hence the signed total tensor of bounded representatives computes $A\otimes^L_kB$ independently of the representatives. Step 3 (internal Hom). For a bounded-below injective replacement $B\to I_B$ and a bounded representative $A$, put $R\mathcal Hom(A,B)=\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,I_B)$ with $d(\varphi)=d_I\varphi-(-1)^n\varphi d_A$; each $\mathcal Hom(A^p,I^q)$ is injective because it is right adjoint to the exact functor $-\otimes A^p$, the total complex is bounded below and termwise injective, and replacing $A$ or $I_B$ changes it only by a quasi-isomorphism (test on the open extensions $j_U!$ and use stalk exactness). This is the actual internal derived Hom, not a sectionwise Hom of stalks. Step 4 (flasque acyclicity). An injective $k$-sheaf is flasque since $\operatorname{Hom}(j_U!k_U,I)=I(U)$ and injectivity extends sections along $j_U!k_U\to j_V!k_V$ for $U\subset V$. Embed a flasque $F$ into an injective $I$; the flasque-kernel lifting theorem ([[lem-flasque-kernel-lifts-quotient-sections]]) makes the quotient flasque with $I(U)\to Q(U)$ onto for every open $U$, so the long exact sequence gives $H^1(U,F)=0$ and $H^{n+1}(U,F)\cong H^n(U,Q)$; induction on degree proves vanishing, and for a bounded-below flasque complex the same degreewise comparison computes derived sections on each open by the ordinary section complex. Step 5 (adjunction identities). The signed chain transposition $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(C\otimes A,I)\cong\mathcal Hom^\bullet(C,\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,I))$ is an isomorphism (Koszul reordering), and since $I$ and $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,I)$ are K-injective and bounded $C$ is K-flat, $H^0$ yields tensor $\dashv$ $R\mathcal Hom$ on $D^b$ with bounded-below target; restriction to opens gives the internal version, and associativity, symmetry, evaluation and currying hold on pure tensors and hence on sheaves. No constructibility of the internal Hom is asserted; that is supplied later on this page by the geometric finite conical/cochain models and the derived incidence model, which are not prerequisites of this lemma.

items.title: Complex algebraic morphisms admit compatible finite smooth stratifications
items.statement:
Assume AC. Let $f:X\to Y$ be one morphism of reduced separated complex
algebraic varieties of finite type
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]), and
prescribe finitely many closed algebraic subsets of each. There are finite
partitions of $X$ and $Y$ into irreducible smooth locally closed algebraic
strata such that every prescribed subset is a union of strata, every stratum
closure is a union of strata of no larger dimension with its boundary of
strictly smaller dimension, and each source stratum maps surjectively and
smoothly onto one target stratum. On analytic spaces each such restriction is a
submersion. The source may be empty. This assertion imposes no Whitney
condition, conical control or topological triviality.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 We record a partition construction. Let $Z$ be a reduced separated complex algebraic variety of finite type and let $\mathcal C$ be a finite list of closed subsets of $Z$. There is a finite partition of $Z$ into irreducible smooth locally closed strata such that every member of $\mathcal C$ is a union of strata and every stratum is open dense in its own irreducible closure. If $Z=\varnothing$ take the empty partition. Otherwise let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_m$ be the irreducible components of $Z$, finitely many by [F1]. Remove from $Z_i$ its nonsmooth locus, the other components $Z_j$, and every $C\cap Z_i$ with $C\in\mathcal C$ and $C\nsupseteq Z_i$. Each removed set is closed, and each is proper in the irreducible $Z_i$; by [F3] and [F2] the nonsmooth locus has smaller dimension, and by [F2] the other removed sets do too, so the result $U_i$ is a nonempty dense open subset of $Z_i$ and is contained in or disjoint from every $C\in\mathcal C$. The $U_i$ are pairwise disjoint and open in $Z$, because their complement is the finite union of the removed closed sets and the sets $Z_j$ with $j\ne i$. The remainder $Z':=Z\setminus\bigcup_iU_i$ is closed and meets each $Z_i$ in a proper closed subset, so $\dim Z'<\dim Z$ by [F2]. Partition $Z'$ by the same construction with $\mathcal C$ replaced by the restrictions of all members of $\mathcal C$ and of all $Z_i$ to $Z'$, and iterate. The dimension of the remainder strictly decreases at every round, so the recursion terminates; because each round respects the restricted lists, every member of $\mathcal C$ is a union of strata and every stratum is open dense in its irreducible closure. [F1, F2, F3, A1, construct]

2.1 Now construct the target strata in rounds on a closed residual subvariety $R\subseteq Y$, starting with $R=Y$; at each stage keep finite lists of prescribed closed subsets of $R$ and of $f^{-1}(R)$, initially the given lists and later those lists enlarged by the restrictions of the closures of all previously emitted strata. Apply step 1.1 to $f^{-1}(R)$ with the maintained source list, obtaining a finite partition into irreducible smooth locally closed strata $Z_\alpha$. Fix an irreducible component $R_i$ of $R$ and remove from it its nonsmooth locus, the other components of $R$, and every maintained target prescribed closed subset not containing $R_i$; by [F1] this leaves a nonempty dense open subset $V_i^0\subseteq R_i$. For each $\alpha$ the image $f(Z_\alpha)$ is irreducible and lies in a component of $R$, so its closure in $R$ is an irreducible closed subset of some component. If that closure is not $R_i$, then its intersection with $R_i$ is a proper closed subset, and we remove it from $V_i^0$; if the closure equals $R_i$, then $f|_{Z_\alpha}$ is dominant, $Z_\alpha$ is smooth and irreducible, and [F4] supplies a dense open subset of $R_i$ over which $Z_\alpha\to R_i$ is smooth, with nonempty fibres over the closed points after shrinking to lie in the image. There are finitely many $\alpha$, so intersecting $V_i^0$ with all these dense opens (and with the images) produces a nonempty dense open $V_i\subseteq R_i$ such that every $Z_\alpha$ whose image closure is not $R_i$ has no point over $V_i$, while every $Z_\alpha$ whose image closure is $R_i$ maps smoothly and onto $V_i$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Emit the target strata $V_i$ of this round and, for every $\alpha$ whose $Z_\alpha$ maps onto $R_i$, the source stratum $S_{\alpha,i}:=Z_\alpha\cap f^{-1}(V_i)$, which is nonempty. It is open in $Z_\alpha$ because $V_i$ is open in $R_i$ and $Z_\alpha\subseteq f^{-1}(R_i)$, hence it is an irreducible smooth locally closed subvariety of $X$, and it maps smoothly and onto $V_i$ as the restriction of the map of step 2.1. Every source point over $V_i$ lies in exactly one such stratum, because the $Z_\alpha$ partition $f^{-1}(R)$ and their intersections with $f^{-1}(V_i)$ are exactly the emitted pieces; those with other image closures have empty intersection by step 2.1. Within the round, closures behave as in step 1.1: the closure of $S_{\alpha,i}$ meets $f^{-1}(V_i)$ in the union of the strata $S_{\beta,i}$ with $Z_\beta\subseteq\overline{Z_\alpha}$, since $f^{-1}(V_i)$ is open in the closed set $f^{-1}(R_i)$. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 Put $R':=R\setminus\bigcup_iV_i$; it is closed and has $\dim R'<\dim R$ by [F2], since each component of $R$ lost a dense open subset. Enlarge both lists by the closures of the emitted strata, restrict to $R'$ and $f^{-1}(R')$, and repeat steps 2.1 and 3.1. The target dimension strictly decreases each round, so after finitely many rounds the emitted strata partition $Y$ and $X$. Every emitted stratum $S$ is open dense in its irreducible closure: this holds within each round by step 3.1, because the pieces of the frontier partition whose closures contain $S$ are contained in $\overline S$ and dense in it; and the maintained lists, which contain the closure of $S$ in every later round, force every later stratum to be contained in or disjoint from $\overline S$. Consequently $\overline S$ is a union of strata, and every stratum $P\subseteq\overline S\setminus S$ has $\dim P<\dim S$: indeed $\overline P$ is an irreducible closed subset of $\overline S$ with $\dim\overline P\le\dim S$, equality would give $\overline P=\overline S$, and then $P$ and $S$, being dense opens of the irreducible $\overline P=\overline S$, would meet, contradicting disjointness of strata. Thus every stratum closure is a union of strata of no larger dimension and its boundary has strictly smaller dimension. Every prescribed subset is a union of strata by the invariance maintained in steps 1.1 and 2.1, and the empty source contributes no source strata. [F1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Finally let $S\to T$ be one emitted restriction onto a target stratum. Zero-dimensional smooth strata are locally single points: they are zero-dimensional Noetherian varieties, hence finite sets of closed points, so their analytic charts and maps to a zero-dimensional target require no implicit-function or constant-rank theorem. A standard smooth presentation with no equations already gives open coordinate charts. In the remaining positive-dimensional cases, the stratum $S$ is a smooth complex variety by construction, so by [F3] it is locally standard smooth over $\mathbb C$; the defining equations of a standard smooth presentation near a point have an invertible Jacobian minor, and [F5] turns them into holomorphic charts of $S$ near that point, with holomorphic transition maps. Similarly $T$ carries holomorphic charts. The map $S\to T$ is a morphism of classical varieties, so in these charts its components are restrictions of regular functions on affine charts, hence locally polynomial quotients with nonvanishing denominators in the ambient coordinates and therefore holomorphic in the chart parameters. At every point the differential of $S\to T$ is surjective by the smoothness of the restriction and the criterion of [F5]; since surjectivity onto a target of dimension $n$ is the nonvanishing of some $n\times n$ minor, the rank stays full on a neighbourhood, and the holomorphic constant rank theorem exhibits the map near each point as a linear projection in suitable holomorphic coordinates. Hence the restriction is a submersion of complex manifolds, in particular a submersion of the underlying real smooth manifolds. No properness or topological triviality is used, and AC is inherited exactly through the cited suppliers. [F3, F5, A1, step 3.1, step 4.1]

6.1 Each emitted source and target piece is nonempty and irreducible, so [F6] proves its analytic connectedness. Its analytic closure is its algebraic closure by [F6]; therefore the algebraic frontier bookkeeping of step 4.1 is the analytic frontier condition as well. Combined with step 5.1 this produces finite connected smooth analytic strata with the required frontier and submersion restrictions, while preserving all algebraic compatibility and dimension conclusions. [F6, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1] ∎

items.title: Irreducible complex varieties are analytically connected
items.statement:
Assume AC. Every nonempty irreducible separated complex algebraic variety of
finite type is connected in its analytic topology. For every locally closed
algebraic subset $A$ of a separated finite-type complex variety $X$, the closure
of $A$ in the analytic topology equals its Zariski closure as a set of classical
complex points. In particular smooth irreducible algebraic strata are connected
complex manifolds once their holomorphic charts have been supplied.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 First let $Z$ be irreducible affine with coordinate domain $B$. By [F1] choose $R=\mathbb C[z_1,\ldots,z_d]\subseteq B$ with $B$ finite over $R$. Write $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$. The localization $(R\setminus\{0\})^{-1}B$ is a finite-dimensional $K$-domain; multiplication by a nonzero element is injective and hence surjective, so this domain is a field, equal to $E=\operatorname{Frac}(B)$. If $d=0$, $B$ is a finite-dimensional complex domain and therefore a field; [F2] forces every algebraic element over $\mathbb C$ to lie in $\mathbb C$, so $B=\mathbb C$ and $Z$ is one point. Otherwise [F2] supplies a primitive element $\eta\in E$ over $K$. Write $\eta=b/s$ with $b\in B$, $0\ne s\in R$ and put $\theta=b$; then $K(\theta)=E$, and $\theta$ is integral over $R$ by [F1], using the finite faithful $R[\theta]$-module $B$ (faithfulness follows by evaluating an annihilator at $1$). By [F1] its monic minimal polynomial is $P(z,T)\in R[T]$, of degree $m=[E:K]\ge1$. It is irreducible and separable over $K$. For finitely many $R$-module generators of $B$, express each as a $K$-linear combination of $1,\theta,\ldots,\theta^{m-1}$ and clear the finitely many denominators. This gives $0\ne a\in R$ with $B_a=R_a[\theta]$. Since $P$ is monic, division by $P$ and linear independence of these powers over $K$ identify this algebra with $R_a[T]/(P)$. [given, F1, F2, A1, construct, algebra]

2.1 By separability and [F2], there are polynomials $H,J\in K[T]$ with $HP+J\partial_TP=1$. Clear denominators to obtain $H_0,J_0\in R[T]$ and $0\ne\delta\in R$ with $H_0P+J_0\partial_TP=\delta$. Put $g=a\delta$ and $V=\mathbb C^d\setminus Z(g)$. This set is nonempty because a nonzero polynomial cannot vanish everywhere on $\mathbb C^d$ (induction on $d$ using the finiteness of roots of a nonzero one-variable polynomial). It is path connected: for distinct $v,w\in V$, the polynomial $t\mapsto g(v+t(w-v))$ is nonzero at $t=0,1$, hence has only finitely many zeros; the complex parameter plane minus those zeros has a path from $0$ to $1$, obtained from the straight segment by finitely many small circular detours. Its image connects $v$ to $w$ in $V$. The principal open $U\subseteq Z$ where $g$ does not vanish is, by step 1.1's coordinate algebra, the space $\{(z,t):z\in V,\ P(z,t)=0\}$. All its coordinate identifications and inverses are polynomial quotients, hence analytic homeomorphisms. For each $z\in V$, $P(z,T)$ is monic of degree $m$ and has exactly $m$ distinct complex roots by the Bezout identity and [F2]. The implicit-function theorem [F3] gives disjoint holomorphic graphs near these roots on one common small connected base ball. They exhaust every nearby fibre because there are already $m$ distinct roots of its degree-$m$ polynomial. Thus $U\to V$ is an actual $m$-sheeted holomorphic covering, with no appeal to an unproved normalization or covering comparison. [F2, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Suppose $U=U_1\amalg U_2$ is a nontrivial analytic clopen partition. On each connected small graph of step 2.1 its membership in $U_1$ or $U_2$ is constant. Consequently the number $m_i$ of roots over $z$ belonging to $U_i$ is locally constant on $V$, hence constant since $V$ is connected. Nonemptiness of both pieces implies $1\le m_i<m$ and $m_1+m_2=m$. Define on $V$ the monic polynomials $Q_i(z,T)$ whose roots are precisely the roots on $U_i$ over $z$. Their coefficients are elementary symmetric functions of those roots; the local holomorphic graphs make them holomorphic, and changing the enumeration changes no symmetric function, so these coefficients glue without any chosen global root functions. Pointwise on $V$ one has $P(z,T)=Q_1(z,T)Q_2(z,T)$. [step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Write $P(z,T)=T^m+p_1(z)T^{m-1}+\cdots+p_m(z)$. Every root satisfies $|t|\le1+\sum_j|p_j(z)|$: if $|t|$ exceeds this quantity, then $|t|>1$ and $|t|^m\le\sum_j|p_j(z)||t|^{m-j}\le(\sum_j|p_j(z)|)|t|^{m-1}<|t|^m$, a contradiction. The polynomial coefficients therefore give a bound $|t|\le C(1+\|z\|_\infty)^D$ for some integer $D\ge0$ and $C\ge1$, valid also near $z=0$. Each coefficient of $Q_i$ is a sum of finitely many products of at most $m_i$ such roots; it is locally bounded near $Z(g)$ and has a bound $C'(1+\|z\|_\infty)^{Dm_i}$ on $V$. Apply [F3] to extend each coefficient to all of $\mathbb C^d$. The same bound holds after extension by continuity: the nonzero polynomial $g$ cannot vanish on an ordinary open ball, since that ball contains a product of disks and successively restricting each variable would force all its coefficients to vanish. Hence $V$ is analytically dense in $\mathbb C^d$. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 An entire function $h$ on $\mathbb C^d$ satisfying $|h(z)|\le C'(1+\|z\|_\infty)^N$ for an integer $N\ge0$ is a polynomial. Indeed [F4] on the radius-$R$ polydisc centred at zero gives $|c_\alpha|\le C'(1+R)^N/R^{|\alpha|}$; uniqueness makes the coefficients independent of $R$ by comparison on the smaller common polydisc. Letting $R\to\infty$ forces $c_\alpha=0$ for $|\alpha|>N$. Its expansion therefore is the finite polynomial $\sum_{|\alpha|\le N}c_\alpha z^\alpha$ on every polydisc, hence on all of $\mathbb C^d$. Apply this to step 4.1's coefficients: $Q_i\in R[T]$. The equality $P=Q_1Q_2$ on $V$ is a polynomial identity, since each coefficient of their difference vanishes on a nonempty ordinary open ball and the preceding one-variable restriction argument makes that coefficient the zero polynomial. Both factors have positive degree smaller than $m$, contradicting the irreducibility of $P$ in $K[T]$. Thus $U$ is analytically connected. This argument factors $P$ itself; it does not infer that one of two polynomial factors is zero from their vanishing on different analytic pieces. [F4, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 The open $U$ is Zariski nonempty in the irreducible affine $Z$. If $Z$ has positive dimension, [F5] supplies at each $x\in Z$ an arc tending to $x$ with punctured image in $U$, so $U$ is analytically dense in $Z$. The zero-dimensional case was already a singleton in step 1.1. The closure of a connected set is connected: any clopen separation of its closure would restrict to a separation of the set, putting the set in one closed side and hence its closure there. Therefore $Z$ is analytically connected. For a general irreducible $X$, choose a nonempty affine open $Z\subseteq X$. It is irreducible and connected by the affine case; [F5] makes it analytically dense in $X$ when $X$ has positive dimension. If $X$ has dimension zero, its nonempty irreducible affine opens are singletons; irreducibility forces them to meet, so $X$ is one point. Again connectedness passes to the closure, proving the first assertion. [F5, step 1.1, step 5.1, construct]

7.1 Finally let $A\subseteq X$ be locally closed algebraic, and write $C$ for its Zariski closure. Algebraic closed sets are analytically closed, because their polynomial equations are continuous on affine charts; hence the analytic closure of $A$ lies in $C$. There is a Zariski open $O\subseteq X$ with $A=C\cap O$. For each of the finitely many irreducible components $C_j$ of $C$, the set $A\cap C_j$ is a nonempty open subset: otherwise the dense set $A$ would be contained in the union of the other components, a proper closed subset of $C$. If $\dim C_j>0$, [F5] gives at every point of $C_j$ an arc with punctured image in $A\cap C_j$, proving analytic density there. If $\dim C_j=0$, it is a point by the affine argument and the finite affine-cover property, and nonemptiness of $A\cap C_j$ puts that point in $A$. Thus every $C_j$ lies in the analytic closure, which is therefore exactly $C$. The empty subset has empty closure in both topologies. The final manifold clause only combines this connectedness with supplied holomorphic charts; no chart existence is inferred from irreducibility. [given, F5, step 1.1, step 6.1] ∎

items.title: Complex algebraic boundary points admit normalized curve arcs
items.statement:
Assume AC. Let $V$ be an irreducible complex algebraic variety of positive
dimension ([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]),
let $O\subseteq V$ be a nonempty Zariski open subset and let $z\in V$. There is
an irreducible algebraic curve $C\subseteq V$ through $z$ not contained in
$V\setminus O$. There is also a holomorphic map $\gamma:\Delta\to V$ from a
sufficiently small complex disk, with $\gamma(0)=z$ and $\gamma(s)\in O$ for
all $s\ne0$; here $\Delta$ is a disk centred at $0$ and a map into $V$ is
holomorphic when its coordinate functions in an affine model containing its
image are holomorphic. The arc can be obtained by analytically parametrizing a
point over $z$ in the finite normalization of $C$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Choose an affine open neighbourhood $V_0$ of $z$ in $V$. Then $V_0$ is irreducible of dimension $d=\dim V\ge1$, and $V_0\cap O
e\varnothing$ because two nonempty open subsets of the irreducible $V$ meet ([[def-irreducible-topological-space-and-subset]]). Put $B=V_0\setminus O$; it is closed in $V_0$ and proper. [F3, given, choose]

2.1 By [F2] applied to the coordinate ring $A$ of $V_0$, choose a finite morphism $h:V_0	o\mathbb A^d$ induced by an injection $\mathbb C[t_1,\ldots,t_d]\hookrightarrow A$ with $A$ module-finite over the image; the integer $d$ is $\operatorname{trdeg}_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Frac}(A)=\dim V_0$ by [F3]. For every irreducible component $W$ of $B$ the image $h(W)$ is closed by [F1], and the induced map $\mathbb C[t]/I(h(W))\hookrightarrow A/I(W)$ is finite and injective; hence $\operatorname{Frac}(A/I(W))$ is algebraic over $\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb C[t]/I(h(W)))$, the two function fields have the same transcendence degree, and $\dim W=\dim h(W)$ by [F3]. A finite union of closed sets has dimension the maximum of the dimensions of its irreducible components, so $\dim h(B)=\dim B<d$, the inequality by [F3] since $B$ is a proper closed subset of the irreducible $V_0$. Thus $h(B)$ is a proper closed subset of $\mathbb A^d$ and there is a nonzero polynomial $P$ vanishing on it, or $P=1$ if $B=\varnothing$. [F1, F2, F3, A1, step 1.1]

3.1 Write $a=h(z)$. The Taylor expansion of a nonzero polynomial $P$ at $a$ has a nonzero homogeneous part, and a nonzero polynomial on $\mathbb C^d$ is not identically zero (induction on $d$ using that a nonzero one-variable polynomial has finitely many roots), so there is $w
e0$ with $P(a+tw)$ not the zero polynomial in $t$; if $B=\varnothing$ take any $w
e0$. The affine line $\ell=\{a+tw:t\in\mathbb C\}$ is therefore not contained in $h(B)$. [step 2.1, algebra, choose, A1]

4.1 Let $g_1,\ldots,g_{d-1}$ be linear forms cutting out $\ell$ in $\mathbb A^d$ (no forms occur when $d=1$), and let $C_0$ be an irreducible component of the closed subset $h^{-1}(\ell)\subseteq V_0$ containing $z$; such a component exists because $h(z)=a\in\ell$. Every component of $h^{-1}(\ell)$ has dimension at least $1$: it is a component of the zero set of the $d-1$ pulled-back forms, so its defining prime is minimal over an ideal generated by $d-1$ elements, has height at most $d-1$ by [F3], and $\dim=\dim A-\operatorname{ht}\ge d-(d-1)=1$; for $d=1$ this reads $\dim V_0=1$. Every component has dimension at most $1$ because it maps finitely into the curve $\ell$, so its dimension equals that of its closed image by the dimension comparison of step 2.1. Hence every component is a curve, and $C_0$ is one of them. [F1, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, A1]

5.1 The curve $C_0$ is not contained in $B$: otherwise $h(C_0)\subseteq h(B)$, while $h(C_0)$ is closed in $\ell$, irreducible, and of dimension $1=\dim C_0$ by step 4.1, hence equal to $\ell$, contradicting $\ell
ot\subseteq h(B)$ from step 3.1. Therefore $C_0\cap O=C_0\setminus B
e\varnothing$. The closure $C:=\overline{C_0}$ in $V$ is an irreducible curve through $z$ meeting $O$, so $C
ot\subseteq V\setminus O$. [F3, step 3.1, step 4.1]

6.1 View $C_0$ with its reduced induced structure: it is a reduced finite-type $\mathbb C$-scheme of pure dimension one, so by [F4] it has a finite normalization $
u:C_0^{\mathrm{nu}}	o C_0$, which is surjective by [F1]; choose $z_0\in C_0^{\mathrm{nu}}$ with $
u(z_0)=z$. Then $C_0^{\mathrm{nu}}$ is regular of dimension one and, over $\mathbb C$, smooth. [F1, F4, step 5.1, choose]

7.1 Take an affine chart $\operatorname{Spec}A_0$ of $C_0^{\mathrm{nu}}$ containing $z_0$ and identify it with a closed algebraic set $X=V(I)\subseteq\mathbb C^M$, $I\subseteq\mathbb C[t_1,\ldots,t_M]$. Since $\mathcal O_{X,z_0}$ is a regular local ring of dimension one, [F6] gives $\dim_{\mathbb C}T_{z_0}X=1$; for a finite generating list $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ of $I$ this tangent space is the kernel of the $r	imes M$ Jacobian matrix at $z_0$, so that matrix has rank $M-1$, and some $M-1$ of the $f_i$, say $f_1,\ldots,f_{M-1}$, have an invertible $(M-1)	imes(M-1)$ minor at $z_0$. Put $Z=V(f_1,\ldots,f_{M-1})$ and let $J'$ be their Jacobian. Then $\dim\mathcal O_{Z,z_0}\le\operatorname{edim}\mathcal O_{Z,z_0}=\dim\ker J'(z_0)=M-(M-1)=1$ by [F6], while $\dim\mathcal O_{Z,z_0}\ge\dim\mathcal O_{X,z_0}=1$ because $X\subseteq Z$ induces a surjection of local rings and dimensions do not increase under quotients. Hence $\dim\mathcal O_{Z,z_0}=1$ and it is regular, therefore a local domain. [F3, F6, step 6.1, construct]

8.1 The inclusion $X\subseteq Z$ induces a surjection of one-dimensional local rings $\mathcal O_{Z,z_0}	woheadrightarrow\mathcal O_{X,z_0}$. Its kernel is a prime ideal, and since the source is a one-dimensional local domain, a nonzero kernel would be the maximal ideal with a zero-dimensional quotient, contradicting $\dim\mathcal O_{X,z_0}=1$; so the kernel is zero and $\mathcal O_{X,z_0}\cong\mathcal O_{Z,z_0}$. Write $I(X)=(g_1,\ldots,g_k)$ by [F7]. Each $g_i$ maps to zero in $\mathcal O_{Z,z_0}$, so for each $i$ there is $h_i
otin\mathfrak m_{z_0}$ with $h_ig_i$ vanishing on $Z$; for $h=h_1\cdots h_k
otin\mathfrak m_{z_0}$ all the $g_i$ vanish on $Z\cap\{h
e0\}$, and since $X\subseteq Z$ we get $X\cap\{h
e0\}=Z\cap\{h
e0\}$. [F6, F7, step 7.1]

9.1 If $M=1$, step 8.1 identifies $X$ with an open neighbourhood of $z_0$ in $Z=\mathbb C$, so translation is the required holomorphic chart. For $M>1$, applying [F5] to $Z$ at $z_0$, whose $M-1$ defining functions have rank $M-1$ at $z_0$ by step 7.1, yields a plane domain $A'\subseteq\mathbb C$ and a holomorphic map $\gamma_0:A'	o\mathbb C^M$ whose image is a neighbourhood of $z_0$ in $Z$, with $\gamma_0$ injective and inverse holomorphic; let $c$ be the value of the free coordinate at $z_0$ and replace $\gamma_0$ by $s\mapsto\gamma_0(c+s)$ on a disk $\Delta\subseteq A'-c$ centred at $0$, so that $\gamma_0(0)=z_0$. Shrinking $\Delta$ and using step 8.1, we may assume $\gamma_0(\Delta)\subseteq X$. Composing $\gamma_0$ with the inclusion $X\subseteq C_0^{\mathrm{nu}}$ and with $
u$ gives an arc into $C$; it is nonconstant and holomorphic, because every coordinate function of the affine model $V_0$ pulls back to a regular function on the affine set $X$, is there represented by a polynomial in $t_1,\ldots,t_M$, and substitution of the holomorphic graph coordinates gives a holomorphic function of $s$. The finite normalization of $C$ restricts over the open curve $C_0=C\cap V_0$ to the normalization of $C_0$: both affine descriptions use the same integral closure, localized at the defining open. Thus this parametrizes a point in the normalization of $C$ as stated. [F5, step 7.1, step 8.1, construct]

10.1 It remains to make the punctured arc avoid $V\setminus O$. Since $C_0
ot\subseteq B$ and $B$ is closed in the irreducible curve $C_0$, the set $C_0\setminus O=C_0\cap B$ has dimension $0$ by [F3] and is therefore finite: a classical variety is Noetherian with finitely many irreducible components, and a zero-dimensional irreducible component is a single point. Because $
u$ is finite, each of its fibres is finite: on an affine chart the coordinate ring is a finitely generated module over the base with finite-dimensional reduction modulo a maximal ideal. Hence $F:=
u^{-1}(C_0\setminus O)$ is finite. The chart $\gamma_0$ of step 9.1 is injective, so $\gamma_0^{-1}(F)$ is finite with at most $|F|$ elements; replacing the disk by a smaller concentric disk, we may assume no nonzero parameter in $\Delta$ has $\gamma_0(s)\in F$ (if $z\in O$, the parameter $0$ is not in this preimage either). Then for every $s
e0$ the point $
u(\gamma_0(s))$ lies in $C_0\setminus
u(F)=C_0\cap O\subseteq O$. Thus $\gamma:=
u\circ\gamma_0:\Delta	o V$ is holomorphic with $\gamma(0)=z$ and $\gamma(s)\in O$ for all $s
e0$, and the arc was obtained by parametrizing the point $z_0$ over $z$ in the finite normalization $C_0^{\mathrm{nu}}$. [F4, F7, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 9.1] ∎

items.title: Incidence cochains of a closed interval
items.statement:
Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Stratify the closed interval by its endpoints and open edge. A finite constructible sheaf has vector spaces $V_0,V_1,V_e$ with generization maps $u_0:V_0\to V_e$ and $u_1:V_1\to V_e$. Its actual derived global sections are computed by
$$[V_0\oplus V_1\xrightarrow{u_0-u_1}V_e],$$
in degrees zero and one. Thus a constant sheaf $k$ has cohomology $k$ in degree zero and zero otherwise. Extension by zero of $k$ on the open edge has one copy of $k$ in degree one and zero otherwise.
items.strategy: Direct verification of the incidence model on the three open simplices. The strict face chains have length at most one (the two nonidentity arrows are $0\to e$ and $1\to e$), so the inverse-limit bar model of [[lem-finite-simplicial-constructible-sheaves-have-a-derived-incidence-model]] has degree-zero term $V_0\oplus V_1\oplus V_e$, degree-one term $V_e\oplus V_e$ and differential $(v_0,v_1,w)\mapsto(w-u_0v_0,\,w-u_1v_1)$. An invertible change of the target coordinates (subtract the second output from the first) and the corresponding invertible change of source coordinate turn this complex into the direct sum of a contractible two-term complex $t\mapsto t$ and the asserted two-term complex $[V_0\oplus V_1\xrightarrow{u_0-u_1}V_e]$; this yields the stated computation of the actual derived global sections ([[def-extension-by-zero-abelian-sheaf]], [[def-geometric-realization-of-an-abstract-simplicial-complex]]). For the constant sheaf all three vector spaces are $k$ and both generization maps are the identity, so the difference map is surjective with one-dimensional kernel; for the extension by zero of $k$ on the open edge both endpoint spaces vanish, leaving a single degree-one term ([[lem-constant-sheaf-is-the-sheaf-of-locally-constant-functions]]). The statement and verification are a worked example generated for this page (no source states this exact two-term witness); the method is the one supplied by the incidence lemma.
items.axiom_use: None beyond the AC already assumed by [[lem-finite-simplicial-constructible-sheaves-have-a-derived-incidence-model]]; the computation itself is finite linear algebra.
